member.summary: Base class for modular, serializable blocks that compose complex actions.
member.remarks:
Action blocks let an action expose optional chunks of behavior without growing one very large parameter list. Blocks can be added, swapped, disabled, and reused by custom editor UI while still executing as part of their parent .
Goals:
Re-use blocks instead of copy/pasting code in actions. Blocks can implement OnSceneGUI which are also re-used.
Simplify UI so the user only sees the blocks they're using. Compare this with complex actions in PM1 with their long parameter lists.
Make it easy for the user to add/swap blocks to experiment.
Aid learning. The user will start to recognize blocks.
Speed up development of complex actions.

member.name: M:HutongGames.PlayMaker.BaseAction.GetSummary
member.summary: Gets a short human-readable summary of this action's configured behavior.
member.returns: A natural-language summary string, or to let the editor build a fallback summary from the action's visible fields.

remarks.para: Summaries are a core part of the PlayMaker 2 authoring experience. They let users scan a state and read what each action does without opening the full inspector. Custom actions should override this method when a hand-written sentence is clearer than a generated list of parameters.

Keep summaries concise, deterministic, and focused on the action's configured intent. Avoid reporting transient runtime state, allocating expensive data, mutating fields, or depending on scene objects that may be unavailable in the editor.

Use field tokens in braces, for example {Target}, {Value}, or {StoreResult}, to ask the editor's natural-language formatter to substitute the current display value of a serialized field. Prefer tokens over manually calling ToString() on variables so variable names, constants, and special values are formatted consistently.
Tokens can include a single formatter suffix using {FieldName:formatter}. The summary builder currently recognizes these formatter names:

item.description: output: For variable reference fields that store results. If the variable is assigned, inserts the standard output arrow before the value; if it is unassigned, hides the whole token. Example: Get {Target} {StoreResult:output}.
hide: For variable reference fields whose default value should stay out of the summary. Unassigned values are hidden; recognized defaults such as and EventSystem.current are also hidden.
var: Looks up an FSM variable by name or GUID instead of an action field. Use {VariableName:var}, or {Guid|Fallback Name:var} when a stable GUID is available.
event: Looks up an FSM event by name instead of an action field, for example {FINISHED:event}.
data-field-values: Specialized formatter for data-table field value lists.

Value display formats such as seconds and mouseButton are passed through to the debug-label formatter for variable values. For example, {Delay:seconds} displays a duration with a seconds suffix, and {Button:mouseButton} displays mouse button names for constant button indices.

remarks.para: The special token {PerSecond} is not a field lookup. It adds (Per Second) only when the action is configured to use per-second timing.

Return when the action is not configured well enough to describe, or when the default natural-language fallback would be better than a custom sentence. Return an empty string only when the action intentionally contributes no text, such as a base class that provides an optional suffix for derived summaries.

member.summary: Validates that required parameters are safe for the action to execute.
member.remarks:
This helper is intended to be used only with required fields. Action fields are required unless marked with .
For parameters, this performs a runtime-safe check by calling :
• At edit time: verifies the field is configured (not set to None).
• At runtime: verifies the referenced value is usable (not null / not destroyed), unless the variable is write-only or a value type.
This prevents many common null-reference errors in actions that immediately read or use the parameter value.
Important:
Some actions intentionally operate on null or uninitialized values (for example: watchers, initializers, creators, or "Is Null" style checks). Those actions should NOT rely on CheckParameters for those inputs and should instead check only configuration (e.g. !variableRef.IsNone) or perform custom validation.
In short:
• Use CheckParameters for required inputs that must have a usable runtime value.
• Do not use it for inputs where null/empty is a valid or expected state.

member.name: T:HutongGames.PlayMaker.OptionalFieldAttribute
member.summary: Marks an action field as optional.

remarks.para: PlayMaker action fields are treated as required by default. Add when a field may be left unassigned, set to None, or otherwise omitted without making the action invalid in the editor.

Optional fields should not be passed to , because that helper validates required runtime inputs. Instead, optional inputs should be checked explicitly before use, and optional output variables should be guarded with IsAssigned before writing.

Optional VariableVar<T> fields need extra care. Value-capable refs commonly default to constant mode, and value-type constants are assigned even when they hold default(T). If an action needs to distinguish "left blank" from "set to the default value," model that explicitly with a companion bool, enum, or mode field instead of relying on IsNone, IsAssigned, or HasValue.

Common uses include optional events, optional filters, optional target overrides, and optional write-only store variables. Pair optional store variables with when the action writes to the variable but does not read from it.

member.summary: Strongly typed link to a Variable that survives serialization, prefab overrides, and cross–object references.

remarks.para: Unity cannot serialize references to managed objects (SerializeReference) that live inside another serialized object. When a Variable lives inside a Variables list on an FSM or Template, any SerializeReference field pointing to it is serialized as an inline copy, not a real reference.
This historically caused:

item.description: Variable links becoming serialized object copies.
Reference equality breaking (Controls.Contains(variable)).
Prefab instance overrides being lost during editor sync.
Cross-host links relying on fragile managedReferenceId lookups.
Some systems relying purely on serialized local variables.

remarks.para: This class now provides a hybrid system that supports both modern and legacy data.

item.description: Variables resolve from a target owner using GUID / MRID / Name.
The resolved variable is canonicalized to restore reference equality.
This is the long-term behaviour.
Older data serialized a full Variable instance in _variable.
Some systems relied on this for local-only links.
The field is kept as a fallback so existing projects continue to work.
GUID lookup (preferred)
ManagedReferenceId lookup (legacy cross-host)
Name lookup (migration fallback)

remarks.para: When resolution succeeds, the embedded variable is replaced with the canonical instance from the owner. If no owner is available, the legacy embedded variable is returned.

Some older systems never stored a target owner or managedReferenceId and relied entirely on the serialized variable. Removing it immediately would break existing assets and tests, so it currently remains as a migration bridge.

item.description: _variable is kept as a fallback.
New links should always initialize an owner.
Links auto-upgrade by storing GUID/MRID/Name when resolved.
Editor validation warns about links still using legacy fallback.
Local-only systems migrate to a lightweight LocalVariableLink.
Remove serialized _variable.
Links become purely key-based (GUID/MRID/Name + owner).

remarks.para: Do not remove _variable until all links initialize an owner and local-only systems have migrated. Removing it too early will break legacy assets and prefab overrides.

member.name: T:HutongGames.UIToolkit.Disabler

summary.para: UIToolkit element that disables and enables contents according to the callback. It's equivalent to EditorGUI.DisabledScope. This has a custom contentContainer, so make sure to add children using VisualElement.Add; children added with VisualElement.hierarchy.Add will not be handled by the Disabler. UXML shouldn't have this problem.

This element is specially useful in combination with SerializedObjectExtensions.IsEditable(SerializedObject) to avoid editing objects that shouldn't be edited. This helps in replicating what happens in IMGUI editors, which become disabled when an object is closed to edit by Version Control or HideFlags.
